title: Push Notification Marketing: Confessions of a Strava Alum - Klaviyo
summary: Build a push notification marketing strategy that works, with real send timing, frequency, and message tactics from a strategist who ran push at Strava.
body_text: Push notification marketing: a real digital strategist's playbook Generated by Klaviyo AI Klaviyo's Jessica Fontanilla, who spent five years managing Strava's marketing tech stack before joining Klaviyo's Professional Services team, breaks down her playbook for mobile push notifications. She covers why push deserves a bigger role in the channel mix, how to grow an opted-in push audience, six message types that work for B2C brands, and how to time, sequence, and test sends across channels. Push has underused advantages: Push lands on the lock screen, carries no per-send cost once a customer has the app, and can drive real revenue — Killstar's push and email flows generated £147,027 in attributed revenue, per the case study cited. Six message types anchor the tactical playbook: Fontanilla recommends time-sensitive alerts, behavior-based nudges (viewed/cart/wishlist/search activity), welcome messages, loyalty and birthday updates, location-based geofencing, and win-back promotions for lapsed customers. Timing and sequencing follow cost and engagement: She advises starting new subscribers at one to two pushes a week, using engagement segments to message active users more often, and sequencing channels — push first, then paid channels like text or WhatsApp, then email — to protect both budget and engagement. Sign up Get a demo Before I joined Klaviyo, I spent 5 years at Strava managing the marketing technology stack for one of the most-loved apps in fitness. At Strava, push notifications are more than a marketing tactic. They’re an actual part of the product experience. You finish a run, you get a notification. A friend gives you kudos, you get a notification. The channel feels natural because it’s built around milestone moments for the user. Then I moved into the broader B2C world at Klaviyo, and I noticed something: most brands treat mobile push notifications as an afterthought. They pour energy into email and text message marketing, launch an app, then send the occasional notification to their push audience, if they send anything at all. That's a missed opportunity, because push has advantages no other channel can match. The average ecommerce app retention rate was only 2.9–3.5% by day 30 in Q2 2026, according to AppsFlyer benchmarks . Push is one of the most direct, lowest-cost ways for brands to re-engage app customers. After nearly a decade in CRM and lifecycle marketing, here's the playbook for mobile push notifications I walk clients through: what to send, when to send it, and who should get it. 4 reasons push notifications deserves a bigger role in your channel mix Push is such an untapped channel. We tend to default to email because it's the bread and butter of so much marketing, but, in the day and age we're in, sometimes the quick snippets are more powerful. Push notifications are different from any other channel in your mix. Here are a few reasons why a mobile push strategy is worth the investment: Your push audience has already raised their hand. Someone who downloads your app and opts into notifications is telling you they want to hear from you. There's far less convincing to do with a push subscriber than with an email subscriber who may have handed over their address for a one-time discount years ago. Push lands on the lock screen. A push notification appears directly on the lock screen, along with other high-priority notifications. When your audience is looking at their phone, a push notification captures attention faster than other channels. Push doesn't add to your send costs. Text messaging and WhatsApp are strong channels, but the per-message costs can add up quickly. Once a customer has your app and opts in, reaching them via push doesn't increase your messaging spend. Push can drive significant revenue for your brand. Gothic lifestyle brand Killstar runs 50 live flows across email and push globally, with push generating £147,027 in attributed revenue . “Incorporating push messaging into Klaviyo alongside email has made our mobile engagement feel complete,” says Chloe Grant, CRM manager at Killstar. “It's helping us reach customers in moments where timing really matters, and we're already seeing the impact.” How to grow your push notification audience Nothing in this playbook matters without opted-in app users, which is where your other channels come in. Your email list, your website, and your social audience are all acquisition engines for your mobile app. Here are a few strategies I regularly recommend to get new app users: Add an app-specific email to your welcome flow. A dedicated message (“Did you know we have an app? Download it for exclusive offers”) converts new subscribers into app users at a high-interest moment. Give your audience a reason to download your app. App-exclusive drops, app-only discounts, and early access make downloading feel like joining an inner circle. Use on-site pop-ups to promote your app. Your website visitors are already engaged. A well-targeted sign-up form pointing to the app captures them without adding costs. Point organic and paid social campaigns to your app. Your social audience is already on their phone, one tap away from your app store listing. It's the shortest possible path from ad to install. 6 push notification marketing tactics that work for B2C brands With push notifications, you only get two lines of text, so you have to make each message count. These are 6 types of messages I see working well for B2C brands: 1. Time-sensitive alerts Push notifications, text messages, and WhatsApp messages are built for need-to-know, minute-by-minute communication. If a message can wait until someone checks their inbox, it can probably be an email. If it can't, it's a strong candidate for push. Think flash sales, back-in-stock alerts, and price drops. Here’s an example of a price drop push notification from apparel brand Yours Clothing , which uses bold font and emojis and personalizes the message to the recipient’s size. Source: Yours Clothing The technical advantage to these messages is deep linking. With deep links , you can route a customer from the notification to the exact product or page inside your app, not to a browser window they have to navigate through. Announce a price drop, link straight to the product, and the path to check-out gets dramatically shorter. Plus, once someone is in your app, they tend to stay and browse. 2. Nudges based on shopping behavior You can trigger a push notification for every behavioral event your app tracks, like: Viewed a product: Browsing behavior powers abandonment flows, price-drop triggers, and up-sell nudges, like, “Still thinking about the Luna boots? 👀 They're 20% off for the next 24 hours.” Added to cart but didn't buy: Cart activity drives abandoned cart pushes and can help you time an up-sell while intent is high. You can pair the push with an in-app message targeted to the same segment, like, "The Harper hoodie in your cart misses you! 🛒 Check-out takes 30 seconds." Added to a wishlist: A wishlist event is one of the strongest purchase signals available. Use it for price-drop pushes and wishlist reminder flows that say, “That item you saved is back in stock,” or “Wishlist alert: The Celeste dress dropped from $59 to $39. You saw it first!” Searched your app or site: Search activity tells you what a customer wants in their own words. If someone searched for something you don't carry yet, or misspelled something you do, a follow-up push can rescue a session that would otherwise end in frustration, like, “Looking for the Nova set? 🔍 It's back, with new colors!” Here’s an example of an abandonment push notification from fashion brand Princess Polly , which encourages the recipient to do a “double take” at the denim they were eyeing earlier. Source: Princess Polly 3. Welcome messages For customers who are new to your app, a simple welcome push (“Welcome to the app, here's what's new”) starts the relationship off on the right foot. It also teaches them what kind of value your notifications will deliver, which is important for setting expectations. Here’s a great example from Killstar that keeps the message short and sweet, encouraging the recipient to use a discount code to get 20% off their first in-app order. Source: Killstar 4. Loyalty and birthday updates Your long-tenured, more engaged app users are a great audience for loyalty messaging like points balances, earned rewards, and birthday perks. If your loyalty program runs on a separate platform from your CRM, a loyalty integration can pull that data into your customer profiles so you can send push notifications. 5. Location-based messages If your brand has physical locations, geofencing can target app users who’ve shared their location based on where they are or where they shop. A geofence identifies the boundary around a specific location, after which you can track when a person enters or exits that boundary and automatically send a push notification. Here are two location-based push notification strategies I recommend: Trigger flows on entry and exit. Send a welcome offer or in-store deal the moment a customer walks in. If they left without purchasing, follow up a few hours later to convert them online. Build location segments. Segment profiles by geofence entry to know who visited which stores, then use those segments for location-specific campaigns. People who entered your New York City store in the last 90 days, for example, get a campaign featuring local events and promotions. Source: Klaviyo Help Center 6. Win-back promotions Push is a low-risk way to re-engage the customers who’ve ghosted you. This is the use case I recommend most often. Emailing unengaged subscribers risks spam complaints and deliverability damage, and text and WhatsApp messages cost money and can feel intrusive to someone who's already drifting away. But if a customer hasn't engaged or purchased in 60–90 days, a push notification is a free test. If they engage, you've won them back at no cost. If they don't, you have a clear signal that it's time to say goodbye. Either outcome makes your program healthier. In this example, Daily Harvest sends a push notification with a win-back reward: 15% off the recipient’s next box when they spend $100. Source: Daily Harvest When to send push notifications: timing, frequency, and channel order Push notification timing comes down to 3 decisions: the time of day, how often you send, and where push sits in your channel sequence. Here’s what to keep in mind: Optimize send time by recipient and intent For scheduled campaigns, deliver at each recipient's local time. You can take this further with personalized send time , which delivers each campaign when someone is most likely to open and tap based on their own engagement history. For triggered flows, the behavior sets the timing: a back-in-stock or cart abandonment push fires the moment it's relevant. This is part of why behavior-triggered flows see more engagement than scheduled campaigns at every stage of the funnel, according to Klaviyo's 2026 Omnichannel Benchmark Report . Either way, give each push a clear objective, like a launch, a sale, or a behavioral trigger, rather than filling a slot on the calendar. Start conservatively with frequency For your new subscribers, start with one or two pushes a week. Sending too many notifications early on tends to drive the most opt-outs, before users have the chance to build a habit with your brand. With engagement-based segments, you can message your most active subscribers more often and send less to anyone who hasn't opened in 60–90 days. You can also cap profiles at one push per configurable window even if multiple campaigns fire at once with Smart Sending . Sequence your channels by cost and customer engagement When a message could go out on push, text messaging, WhatsApp, or email, you have some options for deciding which channel goes first: Think about cost. Push has no per-send cost. After sending a push notification, you can escalate to a paid messaging channel like text or WhatsApp, then finally email the customers who haven’t engaged yet. Think about channel preference. Use AI-powered channel affinity to identify which channel each customer is most likely to engage on next, and let your campaign or flow start there instead. With the cost approach, you’re protecting your budget. With the affinity approach, you’re protecting engagement. Either way, you’re protecting your customers, so they get the right message at the right time. I recommend you start with push where you can, because it’s included in your Klaviyo plan. You can send it to as many people as you want. If they don’t interact, send a text or WhatsApp message, depending on where your customer is and what they use. You can reuse similar messaging, but you're saving on the cost because you already tried push. Still nothing? Send an email. That ranking increases the ROI on your spend. How to measure and test your push notification strategy Push metrics need a different lens than email. Because a notification shows its full message on the lock screen, a customer can read it, never tap, and still convert on your site an hour later. So track opens, clicks, and deliverability, but also track influence. Look at mobile purchases shortly after a send. Then, put your energy into testing. With only two lines to work with, small copy changes can have a big impact. A/B test push messages within flows and let the results guide your strategy. Here are some ideas for A/B testing to increase push notification opens : Personalized vs. generic Test whether dynamic content like a name, a saved product, or a nearby store actually increases taps over a one-size-fits-all message. For example: A: "Back in stock: the Mara jacket you saved." B: "New arrivals just dropped!" Curiosity vs. urgency Test hooks in your messaging. Find out which ones your audience responds to before using similar hooks in text messages, WhatsApp, or emails. For example: A: "Something special is waiting for you. 👀" B: "4 hours left: 20% off everything." Rich vs. plain Test whether emojis, images or GIFs , and sounds help, or if they just add noise for your audience. For example: A: “🚨 Restock alert: the Daisy dress is back 🖤 Your size won't last long.” Test with a photo of the dress and a notification sound, all in isolation. B: “Restock alert: the Daisy dress is back. Your size won't last long.” Send text only without a sound. Anchor your analysis on positive engagement trends. Are opens and clicks holding steady as your audience grows? Are opt-outs staying flat as you adjust frequency? If engagement dips, treat it as an early warning system and pull back before customers opt out. With Klaviyo, push notifications pull in customers Your push subscribers gave you prime real estate: their phone lock screen. Send them messages that are timely, personal, and worth their attention, and they'll keep that line open. Klaviyo mobile app marketing runs alongside your email, text message, and WhatsApp marketing in the same B2C CRM , with unlimited messages included in any Klaviyo plan. That means you can: Send behavior-triggered pushes from the flows you already use. Add push to your abandoned cart, back-in-stock, price-drop, and win-back flows , and A/B test push messages to improve performance over time. Route every message to each customer's preferred channel. Channel affinity predicts where your customers are most likely to engage next, so your cross-channel sequencing starts on the best channel automatically. Send customers exactly where you want them to go. Deep links route customers straight to a product page or cart inside your app, and smart sending windows keep push notifications, text messages, and emails from stacking up on the same customer in the same hour. Greet shoppers when they arrive. Pair push with in-app messages that target the same users. Put your app to work with Klaviyo mobile app marketing. title: Canaan Inc. to Repurchase Shares Using Portion of Digital Asset Treasury
summary: Repurchases will be executed under the Company's existing share repurchase authorization SINGAPORE, Aug. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Canaan Inc. (NASDAQ: CAN) ("Canaan" or the "Company"), an innovator in compute and energy infrastructure, today announced that it has authorized its management to
body_text: Repurchases will be executed under the Company's existing share repurchase authorization SINGAPORE , Aug. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Canaan Inc. (NASDAQ: CAN) ("Canaan" or the "Company"), an innovator in compute and energy infrastructure, today announced that it has authorized its management to monetize a portion of its digital asset treasury to fund repurchases of its American depositary shares ("ADSs") under the share repurchase program authorized by its board of directors (the "Board") effective December 12, 2025. The Company may fund further repurchases using its digital asset proceeds, depending on the trading price of its ADSs, prevailing market conditions, working capital requirements, and other considerations. Any such action remains subject to Board oversight and to the limits of the existing authorization. This approach reflects Canaan's disciplined capital allocation strategy, balancing active treasury management with its long-term commitment to maintaining a strategic digital asset treasury. Based on its current market capitalization, the Company is trading below the combined value of its digital assets holdings and its cash and cash equivalents as reported on March 31, 2026, the end of its most recently reported quarter. According to its June 2026 monthly production and mining operation updates, the Company held digital assets with an approximate market value of US$130 million based on prevailing market prices as of August 3, 2026. These assets are held in accordance with the Company's treasury and custody policy. "This decision reflects our disciplined approach to capital allocation and our commitment to creating long-term shareholder value,'' said Nangeng Zhang, chairman and chief executive officer of Canaan. "Our operations continue to generate bitcoin , providing us with a flexible source of capital that we can deploy selectively and with discipline. At current trading levels, we believe Canaan's market value does not fully reflect the value of our digital asset holdings, cash position, and the strength of our underlying business. Using a portion of our digital asset treasury to repurchase shares therefore represents a compelling allocation of capital and demonstrates our confidence in the Company's long-term prospects.'' About Canaan Inc. Established in 2013, Canaan Inc. (NASDAQ: CAN), is a technology company focusing on ASIC high-performance computing chip design, chip research and development, computing equipment production, and software services. Canaan has extensive experience in chip design and streamlined production in the ASIC field. In 2013, Canaan's founding team shipped to its customers the world's first batch of mining machines incorporating ASIC technology under the brand name Avalon. In 2019, Canaan completed its initial public offering on the Nasdaq Global Market. To learn more about Canaan, please visit https://www.canaan.io/ . title: Code, craft, and the making of nested folders
summary: From treating code as a proposal to turning handoffs into conversations, here's how we shaped a new way of working to ship nested folders.
body_text: Today, we’re excited to introduce nested folders , a long-requested feature that helps growing teams keep their files organized as they scale content and tackle complex projects. Nested folders may sound like a straightforward quality-of-life improvement, but building them required rethinking Figma’s underlying content and permissions model from the ground up—everything from the file browser and admin controls to sharing, permissions, and core infrastructure. When we started the project a year ago, we followed a traditional product development process: Product worked through the requirements, design mapped the experience, and engineering began building once the thinking felt resolved. Midway through the project, the context changed. On the one hand, our team was pursuing new AI-native capabilities that divided our resources. On the other, tools like Figma Make A properties panel and annotations, now in Figma Make With visual editing and annotations, Figma Make is bridging the gap between design and code. Select any element you want to change, adjust it directly in the properties panel, or write in-context prompts with annotations. , the Figma MCP server 4 ways we’re using our MCP server at Figma The Figma MCP server reaches further across the platform than it ever has. From updating a living deck to shipping a design to production—here's what that looks like in practice. , agent skills Got skills? Make the Figma agent a better collaborator From sharing your best thinking to learning from your team’s go-to prompts, here’s what skills unlock in the Figma agent. , codebase prototyping Figma Make, now on your local code From visual editing to contextual prompting and collaboration, Figma Make is expanding how teams can design with code. , and context-aware agents Figma’s design agent, now with custom tools and greater context Prompting gets you started. Custom tools, real context, and skills take the design agent further—so what ends up on the canvas actually looks like you. were making it much faster to turn an idea into something tangible. We could start building anywhere: with a prototype, code, or even something scribbled in Slack. A Figma workspace organized with nested folders. To match these shifts and ship nested folders, we leaned into a new way of working: Led with code: As code became cheaper to produce, we moved faster by spinning up pull requests (PRs) to test our ideas instead of getting lost in theoretical discussions. Shifted responsibilities: We worked with flexibility to address each problem, so engineers made design calls, our designer pushed code, and our product manager traded day-to-day execution for tackling bigger strategic questions. Exchanged handoffs for conversations: Blurring roles made us students and teachers in turn, and sharing the parts of our craft we used to guard built the trust the work needed. Here’s how those changes looked from three perspectives across engineering, design, and product. Together, they show how our team found ways to deepen the relationships supporting the work, combined skillsets, and stayed focused on shipping the right experience or solution. Software Engineer Ethan Adams on reaching new velocity with code A few months into this project I realized that the typical product development process would take too long. It was like being halfway through a final exam, looking up, and discovering that there were only five minutes left on the clock—we had to move faster. Rather than debating product requirements (“Who should have access to X?”) in sprawling Slack threads or meetings, we led with code as the proposal. These discussions had been valuable prerequisites when writing code was expensive and time-consuming, but we're in the era of agents. Instead of guessing if an idea would work, we simply spun up a PR to prove it. We merged code as long as it didn’t break anything. This made it possible for us to quickly sketch ideas and show them to our cross-functional partners in a real, live testing ground. Copy not perfect? No worries. Functionality lacking? That was alright. Logical gaps? We could fix those later! In practice, this was a huge unlock for our velocity, and built confidence in the proposals we eventually selected. A working demo in your actual codebase beats a Product Requirements Document (PRD) every time. Even though I had the green light to make product decisions as an engineer, I still relied on our Product Manager Sachi Shah as a thought partner to share ownership. Our collaboration used to look like a waterfall: She decided a requirement, and I implemented it. This time, it looked more like a verification loop: I led with a proposal, merged prototypes into staging, solicited feedback from Sachi, smoothed out the rough edges, and finally deployed the finished product. Instead of long, drawn-out Slack threads, folks like Software Engineer Julia Sun would proactively put up ideas on staging for us all to test.​​​​‌﻿‍﻿​‍​‍‌‍﻿﻿‌﻿​‍‌‍‍‌‌‍‌﻿‌‍‍‌‌‍﻿‍​‍​‍​﻿‍‍​‍​‍‌﻿​﻿‌‍​‌‌‍﻿‍‌‍‍‌‌﻿‌​‌﻿‍‌​‍﻿‍‌‍‍‌‌‍﻿﻿​‍​‍​‍﻿​​‍​‍‌‍‍​‌﻿​‍‌‍‌‌‌‍‌‍​‍​‍​﻿‍‍​‍​‍‌‍‍​‌﻿‌​‌﻿‌​‌﻿​​‌﻿​﻿​﻿‍‍​‍﻿﻿​‍﻿﻿‌‍‌‍‌‍‍‌‌‍‌﻿‌‍﻿‌‌‍​‌​‍﻿‍‌﻿​﻿‌‍​‌‌‍﻿‍‌‍‍‌‌﻿‌​‌﻿‍‌​‍﻿‍‌﻿​﻿‌﻿‌​‌﻿‌‌‌‍‌​‌‍‍‌‌‍﻿﻿​‍﻿﻿‌‍‍‌‌‍﻿‍‌﻿‌​‌‍‌‌‌‍﻿‍‌﻿‌​​‍﻿﻿‌‍‌‌‌‍‌​‌‍‍‌‌﻿‌​​‍﻿﻿‌‍﻿‌‌‍﻿﻿‌‍‌​‌‍‌‌​﻿﻿‌‌﻿​​‌﻿​‍‌‍‌‌‌﻿​﻿‌‍‌‌‌‍﻿‍‌﻿‌​‌‍​‌‌﻿‌​‌‍‍‌‌‍﻿﻿‌‍﻿‍​﻿‍﻿‌‍‍‌‌‍‌​​﻿﻿‌​﻿​‌‌‍‌‌‌‍​‌​﻿​﻿​﻿​﻿​﻿​‌​﻿​﻿‌‍‌​​‍﻿‌‌‍​‌‌‍‌‍​﻿‍​​﻿​﻿​‍﻿‌​﻿‌​​﻿‍​‌‍​‍​﻿​‌​‍﻿‌‌‍​‍​﻿‍​​﻿‌﻿‌‍​‍​‍﻿‌‌‍​‌​﻿‌‍‌‍‌‍​﻿‌​​﻿‌‍‌‍​‌​﻿​﻿​﻿​‌‌‍​‍‌‍‌‍​﻿​‌​﻿‍‌​﻿‍﻿‌﻿‌​‌﻿‍‌‌﻿​​‌‍‌‌​﻿﻿‌‌‍‌‍‌‍‍‌‌‍‌﻿‌‍﻿‌‌‍​‌‌​​‍‌‍﻿​‌‍﻿﻿‌‍‌﻿‌‌​​‌‍﻿﻿‌﻿​﻿‌﻿‌​​﻿‍﻿‌﻿​​‌‍​‌‌﻿‌​‌‍‍​​﻿﻿‌‌‍​﻿‌‍﻿﻿‌‍﻿‍‌﻿‌​‌‍‌‌‌‍﻿‍‌﻿‌​​‍‌‌​﻿‌‌‌​​‍‌‌﻿﻿‌‍‍﻿‌‍‌‌‌﻿‍‌​‍‌‌​﻿​﻿‌​‌​​‍‌‌​﻿​﻿‌​‌​​‍‌‌​﻿​‍​﻿​‍‌‍‌​‌‍‌​​﻿​‍​﻿​‍​﻿​​‌‍​﻿‌‍‌‍‌‍‌‍‌‍‌​​﻿​﻿‌‍‌‍​﻿​​​‍‌‌​﻿​‍​﻿​‍​‍‌‌​﻿‌‌‌​‌​​‍﻿‍‌‍​‌‌﻿​﻿‌﻿​﻿‌‍‌‌‌﻿‌​‌﻿​﻿​‍‌‌​﻿‌‌‌​​‍‌‌﻿﻿‌‍‍﻿‌‍‌‌‌﻿‍‌​‍‌‌​﻿​﻿‌​‌​​‍‌‌​﻿​﻿‌​‌​​‍‌‌​﻿​‍​﻿​‍​﻿​‌‌‍​‌‌‍‌‍​﻿‌﻿​﻿‌​​﻿‌​​﻿‍​​﻿‍​​﻿‌﻿​﻿​​​﻿​‌​﻿​‍​‍‌‌​﻿​‍​﻿​‍​‍‌‌​﻿‌‌‌​‌​​‍﻿‍‌‍​﻿‌‍​‌‌﻿​​‌﻿‌​‌‍‍‌‌‍﻿﻿‌‍﻿‍​﻿﻿﻿‌‍​‍‌‍​‌‌﻿​﻿‌‍‌‌‌‌‌‌‌﻿​‍‌‍﻿​​﻿﻿‌‌‍‍​‌﻿‌​‌﻿‌​‌﻿​​‌﻿​﻿​‍‌‌​﻿​﻿‌​​‌​‍‌‌​﻿​‍‌​‌‍​‍‌‌​﻿​‍‌​‌‍‌‍‌‍‌‍‍‌‌‍‌﻿‌‍﻿‌‌‍​‌​‍﻿‍‌﻿​﻿‌‍​‌‌‍﻿‍‌‍‍‌‌﻿‌​‌﻿‍‌​‍﻿‍‌﻿​﻿‌﻿‌​‌﻿‌‌‌‍‌​‌‍‍‌‌‍﻿﻿​‍‌‍‌‍‍‌‌‍‌​​﻿﻿‌​﻿​‌‌‍‌‌‌‍​‌​﻿​﻿​﻿​﻿​﻿​‌​﻿​﻿‌‍‌​​‍﻿‌‌‍​‌‌‍‌‍​﻿‍​​﻿​﻿​‍﻿‌​﻿‌​​﻿‍​‌‍​‍​﻿​‌​‍﻿‌‌‍​‍​﻿‍​​﻿‌﻿‌‍​‍​‍﻿‌‌‍​‌​﻿‌‍‌‍‌‍​﻿‌​​﻿‌‍‌‍​‌​﻿​﻿​﻿​‌‌‍​‍‌‍‌‍​﻿​‌​﻿‍‌​‍‌‍‌﻿‌​‌﻿‍‌‌﻿​​‌‍‌‌​﻿﻿‌‌‍‌‍‌‍‍‌‌‍‌﻿‌‍﻿‌‌‍​‌‌​​‍‌‍﻿​‌‍﻿﻿‌‍‌﻿‌‌​​‌‍﻿﻿‌﻿​﻿‌﻿‌​​‍‌‍‌﻿​​‌‍​‌‌﻿‌​‌‍‍​​﻿﻿‌‌‍​﻿‌‍﻿﻿‌‍﻿‍‌﻿‌​‌‍‌‌‌‍﻿‍‌﻿‌​​‍‌‌​﻿‌‌‌​​‍‌‌﻿﻿‌‍‍﻿‌‍‌‌‌﻿‍‌​‍‌‌​﻿​﻿‌​‌​​‍‌‌​﻿​﻿‌​‌​​‍‌‌​﻿​‍​﻿​‍‌‍‌​‌‍‌​​﻿​‍​﻿​‍​﻿​​‌‍​﻿‌‍‌‍‌‍‌‍‌‍‌​​﻿​﻿‌‍‌‍​﻿​​​‍‌‌​﻿​‍​﻿​‍​‍‌‌​﻿‌‌‌​‌​​‍﻿‍‌‍​‌‌﻿​﻿‌﻿​﻿‌‍‌‌‌﻿‌​‌﻿​﻿​‍‌‌​﻿‌‌‌​​‍‌‌﻿﻿‌‍‍﻿‌‍‌‌‌﻿‍‌​‍‌‌​﻿​﻿‌​‌​​‍‌‌​﻿​﻿‌​‌​​‍‌‌​﻿​‍​﻿​‍​﻿​‌‌‍​‌‌‍‌‍​﻿‌﻿​﻿‌​​﻿‌​​﻿‍​​﻿‍​​﻿‌﻿​﻿​​​﻿​‌​﻿​‍​‍‌‌​﻿​‍​﻿​‍​‍‌‌​﻿‌‌‌​‌​​‍﻿‍‌‍​﻿‌‍​‌‌﻿​​‌﻿‌​‌‍‍‌‌‍﻿﻿‌‍﻿‍​‍​‍‌﻿﻿‌ Product Designer Cai Charniga on going from pixels to pull requests I have a confession: My PR count is pretty low for this project. Two, maybe three. I didn’t magically cross over and become an engineer, but we all started stepping into roles that used to exclusively belong to someone else. On this project, the engineers had strong instincts for structure, and a deep understanding of how complex enterprise permissions work inside a tool like Figma, so they regularly came to me with flows and design tweaks. When you have a strong design system giving people guardrails, and enough trust that they feel free to make the call, an engineer can go deep on a design feature and get it to a really solid state. This meant that when someone was at capacity, the work didn’t stall waiting for the right person to pick it up. For example, we were working through our folder sharing flows: how the share modal should communicate inheritance for users with view or edit access, and how to handle the trickier cases where inheritance is broken. Software Engineer Jenny Yu stepped in and mocked up a few options. From there, I brought in our UX writer, Molly Rosen Marriner, and the three of us built on Jenny's approaches on the Figma Design canvas: Jenny keeping the flow technically sound, Molly sharpening the permissions language, and me shaping the visual hierarchy. Sometimes, this is what collaboration on canvas looks like—messy and organic. It ran the other way, too. There were times I picked up a change, got into the code, and realized how much was happening under the hood—enough that I'd go back to the team and say, “Honestly, this one shouldn't be mine.” Knowing where your expertise runs out is its own kind of craft. Even so, I think every designer should try to push a PR. When Ethan set me up with CoderBox, our sandbox for spinning up code environments, I felt how long certain changes took to build before I could even preview them, and that did more for my empathy than any handoff ever had. Engineers could carry design work, and I could get into the code myself. That gave me room to go deep where it counted, running through more versions of the folder UI than the old handoff model would ever have allowed. I used agents like Cursor, often directly in Slack, in order to keep everyone in the loop. Product Manager Sachi Shah on trading control for conviction With this new way of working, the first thing I had to let go of was the assumption that good product thinking had to come exclusively from the PM. My job became matching the right people to the right problems, giving them room to run, and knowing when to step back in. Jenny Yu became one of my closest thought partners on critical content operations like how people move, duplicate, and transfer folders across Figma. Ricky Zein, also a software engineer, owned the experience for individual users and smaller teams, whose needs are often different from those of enterprise customers. And Data Scientists Patrick Kehinde Jr. and Eric Aberbook mapped how the new permissions model would affect each cohort, helping me pressure-test our assumptions and focus on the biggest risks. Letting go of day-to-day execution gave me more time to focus on the strategic question underneath the project: Did better file organization still matter in an AI-first world, or were folders becoming archaic as AI search improved? We built artifacts that helped us see how folders could matter even more as people created more work—giving future AI search richer structure and context to retrieve against. But what helped most was stepping back to build a balanced portfolio of bets. Alongside nested folders, our team sprinted to launch skills in the Figma agent Got skills? Make the Figma agent a better collaborator From sharing your best thinking to learning from your team’s go-to prompts, here’s what skills unlock in the Figma agent. , another part of Figma’s AI-native strategy. Counterintuitively, spending less time PMing every detail gave me more room to build a roadmap where foundational customer needs and new AI-native experiences could move forward together. Within the project itself, the most important place for me to redirect my attention was toward customers. I took on running the early-access program (EAP), and we got really scrappy. At Config Config 2026: New materials, new tools and a more expressive canvas Push past what you thought was possible with code layers, Figma Motion, shaders, generative plugins and Weave tools, all on the canvas. , I crashed happy hours with our team’s Engineering Manager Ayush Mehra to cold-pitch customers on the file-organization system we were building. We convinced several people to join the EAP on the spot. From there, we kept expanding. Friends of Figma A new chapter: Friends of Figma’s brand refresh tells the story of a global community From São Paulo to Seoul, Friends of Figma chapters around the world are distinct, vibrant, and locally rooted. Our new brand gives them a more authentic way to express themselves. communities in Jaipur, Barcelona, Mumbai, and Lahore became early adopters. I also reached out to community leaders around the world and people on X who had been especially vocal about file organization—including Ilya Miskov​ , a designer who had joined one of our early discovery conversations. Customer feedback showed us how nested folders behaved inside live organizations, with messy files and established habits. It helped us catch bugs, fine-tune the experience, and reduce the risk of migrating customers to an entirely new content model. Time in the room with customers gave me a kind of product clarity I couldn’t get from speccing alone. Trading control for conviction required me to step into the work I was best positioned to do, while trusting other people to do the same. This way of working only works when the team trusts one another. Candidly, blurring roles was awkward: There were moments when we stepped on each other’s toes, crossed a boundary clumsily, or tried something we’d never done before. That discomfort was part of finding a new normal, and we could only move through it because we had invested in the relationships underneath the work. Over time, we became less precious about our individual domains and started actively teaching one another the parts of our craft we had previously held most closely. We kept trust and context intact through shared rituals: weekly bug bashes, cross-functional syncs, live pairing between design and engineering, and celebrations of major milestones—including launching internally to all of Figma. Those rhythms kept us anchored on the same goal, delivering on an eagerly anticipated customer promise without compromising quality. Nested folders will take a few weeks to roll out to all users. Visit our help center to learn more about how to get started. Ethan Adams is an engineer at Figma. He holds the rare hat-trick accomplishment of holding a patent, publishing a peer-reviewed research paper, and releasing an EP to millions of listeners. LinkedIn Sachi Shah is a product manager at Figma. She came to product by way of a degree called Leadership in Creative Enterprise, which she designed at Carnegie Mellon. title: Written in Code: This code is building rails for the world's banks.
summary: Galaxy builds the custody, staking, and tokenization infrastructure behind the world's leading banks and asset managers. This is what runs underneath.
body_text: Institutional-grade onchain infrastructure for traditional financial institutions. Programmable rails. The economy that runs on code needs rails. Galaxy is building them with some of the largest institutions in finance. Code already rewrote how information moves. It is now rewriting how value moves. That is the code economy. Money, markets, and ownership become programmable, and the infrastructure beneath them becomes software. For a financial institution, that means the plumbing changes while the products stay familiar. A fund is still a fund. A dollar is still a dollar. What changes is the speed and the hours. Rails that settle in seconds. Markets that do not close on a Friday. Assets that carry their own instructions, so interest can pay itself and compliance can be enforced at the moment of transfer rather than weeks after it. Leading institutions have made their choice. BNY. State Street. Morgan Stanley. BlackRock. Invesco. Each is building on Galaxy infrastructure. Custody is the layer everything else plugs into. An institution cannot trade, stake, tokenize, or report on an asset it is not holding safely. Get that right and the rest of the stack has something to attach to. Galaxy builds that layer. The institution holds its own keys. Vaults stay offline. Signing runs through multi-party computation, so no one person can move anything alone. A policy engine enforces the institution’s own controls, jurisdiction by jurisdiction. That technology does not only run inside Galaxy. Regulated custodians have standardized their own platforms on it. Their clients log in and see their name. The code underneath is Galaxy’s. Staking shows what that foundation buys. It once meant moving assets out of the vault and trusting whoever received them. Now they stay where they are and earn. Whoever runs the validator still has to run it well. Blockchains penalize failure automatically. A validator that drops offline stops earning. One that signs the wrong thing is slashed, and the stake absorbs the loss. Galaxy runs its own, has operated one of the largest Solana validator operations in the world, and puts slashing protection and institutional insurance behind them. Tokenization sits on the same foundation. Galaxy’s technology powers SWEEP , the tokenized liquidity fund launched with State Street Investment Management. Galaxy was the first public company to tokenize its SEC-registered shares directly on a public blockchain . Not a wrapper. The actual stock, moving onchain. That record is why institutions ask Galaxy to build theirs. Engineers deploy into the institution’s own environment and build on its systems. At handover, the institution owns the platform outright. Galaxy stays to run it and extend it. The names on these platforms will vary. The rails underneath will not. The more of this economy gets built, the more of it runs on Galaxy. Grow the economy that runs on code. ©Galaxy Holdings LP. 2026. All rights reserved.

title: How to Build an AI Video Car Damage Inspector
summary: Upload one slow walkaround video of a rental car and get back a signed, timestamped report of every scratch and dent, with reflections filtered out by physics. Here's how to build it with RF-DETR, Roboflow Workflows, and Gemini.
body_text: Aarnav Shah Published Aug 7, 2026 • 6 min read Summary This tutorial builds a rental-car walkaround inspector. You upload a video of the car, and the system timestamps it before it even finishes uploading, runs an RF-DETR damage model inside a Roboflow Workflow with ByteTrack tracking, rejects reflections with a custom Python block that tests how each detection physically moves, has Gemini assess or veto every surviving finding, and hands back a digitally signed PDF report that anyone can verify in their browser. If you've ever rented a car, you've probably done your best to document everything about it when you received it. You walked all the way around it, photographing every issue you could find. But maybe three weeks later an email shows up claiming you dented the door, with a repair bill attached. Did you even photograph that panel at all? A folder of camera-roll photos proves much less than it feels like it does. I wanted to fix that with computer vision. My idea was that a user could upload one slow walkaround video of a car, and get back a report that contains when the video was uploaded and descriptions of every scratch and dent. In my app, the detection and tracking run in a Roboflow Workflow on a trained RF-DETR model . While damage assessment and vehicle identification run in two more workflows on hosted Gemini blocks . I'll show you how you can build it, too. Follow along with this GitHub repository . 0:00 / 1:11 Building an AI Video Car Damage Inspector When you pick a video, the app computes its fingerprint and sends only that, about a hundred bytes, to be certified by an independent timestamp authority. This happens before the multi-megabyte upload starts. The video then uploads in resumable chunks, and the server checks that the file it received matches the certified fingerprint exactly. Next, the Roboflow workflow runs the damage detector on every sampled frame, tracks detections across frames with ByteTrack , and hands each tracked box to a custom Python block for the physics test below. Real damage is part of the car's surface, so it moves with the body panel as the camera walks past. A reflection glides across the panel. That takes care of killing most false positives. What's left after that gets a structured assessment by Gemini covering type, severity, approximate size, and affected part, and Gemini can veto a finding as a false positive. The language model can describe or reject findings, but it can never add one, so nothing hallucinated ends up in the signed document. Train the Model I trained RF-DETR-small entirely in the Roboflow UI . Start by forking a car damage dataset on Universe with part-specific damage classes like fender-dent, doorouter-dent, and sidemirror-damage, then kick off training from the dataset page; you never leave the browser. My model achieved a 69.8 mAP50 with 65.5 recall. Since Gemini only ever sees crops of what the detector proposed, a dent the model never detects is invisible to the whole pipeline. But a video recording can make up for this because a dent missed in one frame is usually caught in another and the tracker stitches those into one finding. The best fix is usually to label them newer images, and retrain the model if the pipeline doesn’t work. 0:00 / 1:44 Get the Code Everything lives in one repository: git clone https://github.com/aarnavshah12/walkaround-inspector.git cd walkaround-inspector/web && npm install cd ../pipeline && python3.12 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt The repository contains: web/ — the Next.js PWA: upload flow, report page, verifier page, and the thin API (timestamping, chunked uploads, PDF signing) pipeline/ — the analysis runner and every tunable threshold in one config.py workflows/ — the three Roboflow Workflow definitions, mirrored from the editor Your Roboflow API key and the report-signing key go in web/.env.local, which is gitignored. The signing key is one openssl command, documented in the repo. Build the Workflow My main pipeline is a workflow called walkaround-video-v , and it's three blocks. The object detection model block points at the trained damage model with a custom confidence of 0.2 - deliberately low. Here I optimized for recall since a weak hunch that persists across thirty frames is worth more than a strong hunch in one frame. This detect-low-then-filter-later pattern shows up across inspection pipelines too. The ByteTrack block turns per-frame detections into tracklets. A one-frame glitch doesn't become a finding, because a one-frame glitch never becomes a track. The parallax filter is a custom Python block. For each tracked box, it finds feature points in a ring around the box, which is the surrounding body panel, and measures how that patch moved between frames using optical flow and a homography. That predicts where the box should be if it were glued to the panel. Then it compares the prediction against where the tracker actually put it. Damage stays put and leaves a tiny residual, while a reflection drifts and leaves a big one. On my test footage, real dents scored residuals of 0.002 to 0.005 of the frame diagonal against a reject line of 0.015. Something I learned along the way was that Custom Python blocks don't run on the serverless API, since Roboflow understandably won't execute arbitrary code on its hosted infrastructure. Any workflow that contains one has to run through InferencePipeline instead, which executes the same workflow definition in-process over your video: pipeline = InferencePipeline.init_with_workflow( video_reference=str(video), workflow_specification=spec, on_prediction=sink, workflows_parameters={"det_confidence": 0.2}, ) The two enrichment workflows have no custom code, so they deploy serverless. walkaround-enrich-a is a Gemini block in structured-answering mode, where the output schema is the prompt, with one field per fact I want: damage type, severity, size in cm, affected part, pre-existing indicators, and an is_false_positive verdict, feeding a JSON parser block. walkaround-vehicle-b is the same pattern for make, model, color, and plate. Both use rf_key:account as the API key, which routes Gemini calls through Roboflow's managed key: no Google account, no separate billing, just workspace credits. Seal the Report The finished report is a PDF signed with ECDSA P-256 and has a second timestamp token of its own, so the evidence chain says the video existed at time A and the report about it existed at time B. A public verifier page re-checks everything in the browser, and the PDF stays on the reader's machine. What It Costs to Run Analysis runs locally and free, at about two minutes per ten seconds of 1080p footage on an M-series laptop, GPU-accelerated. The Gemini assessments cost a few Roboflow credits per video through the managed key. The timestamp authority is free, the model trains on the free tier, and the signing key is an openssl one-liner. There's no per-video cloud bill unless you want one because the same workflow JSON can run on a hosted GPU when it's time to scale. Build Your Own Fork a car damage dataset on Universe and train RF-DETR-small on it, entirely in the UI. Clone the repo, install the web and pipeline dependencies, drop your API key and a signing key in .env.local. Import the three workflow definitions from workflows/ into your workspace, or rebuild them block by block in the editor. Run the web app, upload a ten-second clip of any parked car, and watch the report assemble itself. Check the vetoes against the crops, tune the gate in config.py against your own footage, and retrain on whatever the detector missed. Every video after that gets better. The next time you get a damage-claim email you'll be ready with your report, a certified timestamp, and a verifier page that settles it in one drop of a file! Further reading: Automate Pothole Detection with RF-DETR and ByteTrack What is ByteTrack? A Deep Dive Pipe and Tube Quality Inspection with RF-DETR Cite this Post Use the following entry to cite this post in your research: Aarnav Shah . (Aug 7, 2026). Honeywell Technologies to Skill 3 Lakh Students Across India in AI, Cybersecurity & Sustainability by 2030
summary: Advancing the STEM ecosystem across India with strategic partners including IIT Bombay, BharatCares, Ladli Foundation, and FSID–IISc
body_text: INDIA, August 11, 2026: Honeywell Technologies (NASDAQ:HON) today announced a major skilling commitment in India, aiming to equip over 3 lakh students with future-ready capabilities in artificial intelligence (AI), cybersecurity, sustainability, and advanced technologies by 2030 under its flagship initiative, Saksham. Over the last 10 years, Honeywell Technologies has already transformed the lives of 13+ lakh beneficiaries, making education more inclusive and future focused. To deliver the large-scale skilling programs, school transformation initiatives, and innovation-led interventions that will impact 3 lakh students across India, Honeywell Technologies is partnering with the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Bombay, BharatCares, the Ladli Foundation and the Foundation of Science, Innovation and Development, an arm of the Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore (FSID-IISc). As industries accelerate adoption of digital and sustainable technologies, building a future-ready workforce has become critical to sustaining economic growth and competitive advantage. However, India is witnessing a growing gap between industry demand and talent readiness. According to the India Skills Report 2026 [1] , (published by ETS in collaboration with CII, AICTE, and AIU) [2] , employability has risen to 56.35%, yet demand for skills in AI, data, cloud and cybersecurity continues to outpace talent supply. “India’s growth and competitiveness depend on how effectively we bridge education and employability at scale,” said Ashish Modi, President, Honeywell Technologies India & APAC . “Through Saksham, Honeywell Technologies is bringing together academia, government, non-profits and industry to create stronger linkages between education, skills and employment. From smart classrooms and sustainability learning to Centres of Excellence and startup incubation, these initiatives are designed to deliver measurable, long-term impact and widen access to opportunity for students across India. Saksham reflects our commitment to advancing the vision of Viksit Bharat by building a future-ready talent and innovation pipeline for the country.” To bridge the gap between talent demand and readiness in India, key skilling programs under Saksham include: 1. IIT Bombay–Honeywell Technologies Centre of Excellence for Future Skills & Innovation The centre will reach over 1 lakh undergraduate students across the country through its network of colleges on expert-led courses across five tracks – Sustainability Reporting, Sustainable Finance, Energy Security, Sustainability Infrastructure, and Policy Advocacy. It will also support applied research projects, research fellows, and startup incubation, strengthening industry-academia collaboration. 2. Honeywell Technologies Future Skills Edge Aims to train 2 lakh students in AI and cybersecurity through hybrid, project-based learning, supported by four Centres of Excellence in government institutions in Maharashtra, Haryana, Karnataka and Telangana. Implemented with BharatCares, the program targets 50% women participation and aligns with national initiatives such as Skill India, NEP 2020, and Digital India. 3. Honeywell Technologies Saksham School Transformation Program In partnership with Ladli Foundation, Honeywell Technologies will transform 12 government and government-aided girls’ schools across Maharashtra, Delhi, Haryana, and Karnataka, benefiting more health and hygiene awareness, and leadership development, alongside teacher training and community engagement 4. Startup Incubation and Innovation Support Honeywell Technologies has been working with FSID-IISC since 2018 and by the end of 2030 will support nearly 75 early-stage deep-science startups and Entrepreneurs-in-Residence (EIRs) across areas such as AI, renewable energy, sustainability, cybersecurity, and digitization. Startups will receive seed funding, mentorship, and access to advanced R&D infrastructure, with a focus on founders from underrepresented communities. 5. Prime Minister’s Internship Scheme Honeywell Technologies engages over 50 underprivileged interns every year through the Prime Minister Internship Scheme. The initiative aims to provide graduating students with hands-on industry exposure, mentorship, and practical workplace experience. Bridging the gap between academic learning and industry needs, the program enables upskilling, career readiness, and employability enhancement. The flagship Saksham initiative is implemented through Hometown Solutions India Foundation (HHSIF) – Honeywell Technologies’ philanthropic arm in India. It is designed to expand access to quality STEM education, drive inclusive and sustainable growth, and build a pipeline of future-ready talent aligned with evolving industry needs, while supporting India’s ambition to become a global technology and innovation hub. About Honeywell Hometown Solutions India Foundation Honeywell Hometown Solutions India Foundation (HHSIF) is the non-profit arm of Honeywell Technologies, dedicated to advancing corporate social responsibility initiatives across India. Its focus areas include education, humanitarian relief, and sustainable community development. In education, HHSIF leads STEM-focused skilling programs, supports research at leading institutes, and helps scale deep-science start-ups. In sustainable community development, it works to build resilient communities by strengthening healthcare infrastructure and enabling rural livelihoods, WASH initiatives, and natural resource conservation through technology-led solutions. Honeywell Technologies has also committed to planting one million trees under its Plant the Future program this decade. Since inception, HHSIF has impacted more than 6.6 million lives across 21 states. About Honeywell Technologies Honeywell Technologies is a global, pure-play automation company with a legacy of innovating to help solve the world’s most mission-critical challenges, enhancing the quality of life for people and communities around the world. We serve the building, industrial, and process sectors with a broad portfolio of services, solutions, and products, underpinned by our Honeywell Technologies Accelerator operating system and Honeywell Technologies Forge intelligence layer. By combining the deep domain expertise of our more than 50,000 employees with decades of data from our global installed base, we are uniquely positioned to lead the industrial sector’s transition from automation to autonomy. For more news and information on Honeywell Technologies, please visit Honeywell Technologies Newsroom . title: BitFuFu Reports Unaudited Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results
summary: SINGAPORE, Aug. 17, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- BitFuFu Inc. (“BitFuFu” or the “Company”) (NASDAQ: FUFU), a world-leading Bitcoin miner and mining services...
body_text: SINGAPORE, Aug. 17, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- BitFuFu Inc. (“BitFuFu” or the “Company”) (NASDAQ: FUFU), a world-leading Bitcoin miner and mining services innovator, today announced its unaudited financial results for the quarter ended June 30, 2026. Second Quarter 2026 Financial Highlights Total revenue was $42.8 million, down 62.9% from $115.4 million in the same period of 2025. This substantial decline reflects the combined impact of a 27.5% year-over-year drop in Bitcoin’s price, softening demand for Cloud Mining Solutions, and the Company's deliberate optimization of deployed hashrate. Three Months Ended June 30, 2026 2025 Category ($ in millions) Revenue % of Revenue Revenue % of Revenue Cloud Mining Solutions $ 24.9 58.2 % $ 94.3 81.7 % Self-Mining Operations 14.0 32.7 % 14.8 12.8 % Mining Equipment Sales - 0.0 % 5.2 4.5 % Hosting Revenue and Others 3.9 9.1 % 1.1 1.0 % Total Revenue $ 42.8 100.0 % $ 115.4 100.0 % Net loss was $20.5 million, compared to net income of $47.1 million in the same period of 2025. Adjusted EBITDA (a non-GAAP metric) was negative $18.4 million, which was significantly impacted by fair value loss of $16.9 million resulting from the decrease in the price of Bitcoin. This compared to positive $60.7 million in the same period of 2025, which included a fair value gain of $43.4 million. Combined balance of cash and cash equivalents and digital assets1 were $119.5 million as of June 30, 2026, compared to $177.1 million as of December 31, 2025. “Second-quarter results reflected one of the more challenging operating environments our industry has experienced recently, but they do not change our conviction in BitFuFu's long-term opportunity. We prioritized operational quality and discipline — proactively optimizing our hashrate mix and nearly tripling self-mining production during the period. At the same time, we continued to expand our turnkey hosting services as a growing source of diversified revenue, while deploying next-generation S21 XP miners and actively managing our fleet to maintain high efficiency and protect our unit economics amid market volatility. Importantly, the reduction in managed hashrate during the quarter was not a simple contraction; rather, it was part of a deliberate effort to improve the quality and economics of our capacity. We have secured additional hashrate that restored our total managed hashrate to approximately 20 EH/s by mid-August and provided a stronger foundation for the second half of the year. Going forward, we will remain focused on improving operating efficiency, maintaining capital discipline, and selectively deploying resources where we see attractive long-term economics. We believe these efforts will position BitFuFu to capture opportunities as the market improves and to continue creating long-term value for our shareholders,” said Leo Lu, Chief Executive Officer and Chairman of the Board. 1 The BTC collateral receivables are not included in the balance of digital assets; and BTC was measured at fair value in the Company’s financials for the quarter ended June 30, 2026. Second Quarter 2026 Operational Highlights Total hashrate decreased by 57.7% to 15.3 EH/s as of June 30, 2026, compared to 36.2 EH/s as of June 30, 2025. Power capacity was 273 MW as of June 30, 2026, compared to 728 MW as of June 30, 2025. Bitcoin (“BTC”) held by the Company decreased by 6.8% to 1,671 BTC as of June 30, 2026, compared to 1,792 BTC as of June 30, 2025. This reduction reflects the Company’s ongoing treasury management strategy, under which BTC was sold during the period to support operational needs and hashrate procurement activities. As of June 30, Metric 2026 2025 Power capacity (MW) 273 728 Total hashrate under management (EH/s) ( 1) 15.3 36.2 BTC Holdings ( 2) 1,671 1,792 Three Months Ended June 30, 2026 2025 BTC Produced From BitFuFu self-mining operations 192 143 By customers from cloud-mining solutions ( 3) 255 917 Average BTC produced per day by customers and BitFuFu 4.9 11.7 (1 ) Defined as the hashrate that could theoretically be generated if all miners that have been energized are currently in operation including miners that may be temporarily offline. Hashrates are estimated based on the manufacturers’ specifications. (2 ) Includes 54 BTC as collateral for loans and excludes BTC produced or pledged by cloud-mining customers. (3 ) Defined as the amount of BTC that was produced during the period by customers using hashrate purchased from cloud-mining solutions. Second Quarter 2026 Financial Review Revenue Total revenue in the second quarter of 2026 was $42.8 million, representing a decrease of 62.9% from $115.4 million in the same period of 2025, primarily due to the decline in Cloud Mining Solutions and Mining Equipment Sales revenue. Revenue from Cloud Mining Solutions for the second quarter of 2026 was $24.9 million, a 73.6% decrease from $94.3 million in the same period of 2025. This decline was primarily attributable to lower average selling prices, driven by falling BTC prices, and weaker market sentiment. The substantial year-over-year decrease in the Cloud Mining revenue also resulted in a low net dollar retention rate2 of 24.1% for the second quarter of 2026, primarily reflecting reduced order volumes from existing customers. 2 The net dollar retention rate was calculated as the ratio of recurring revenue in the second quarter of 2026 to total Cloud Mining revenue in the second quarter of 2025. Revenue from Bitcoin self-mining operations in the second quarter of 2026 was $14.0 million, compared with $14.8 million in the same period of 2025. The year-over-year change primarily reflected the combined effect of: (1) higher blockchain network difficulty, which reduced average daily BTC earnings per tera-hash by 9.7%; (2) a 27.5% decline in the average BTC price to $71,600 in the second quarter of 2026 from $98,800 in the second quarter of 2025; and (3) a partially offset from a 47% increase in average hashrate allocated to self-mining operations. Revenue from mining equipment sales was nil in the second quarter of 2026, compared with $5.2 million in the same period of 2025, driven by lower customer demand amid Bitcoin price uncertainty and broader market sentiment. Revenue from Hosting and Other was $3.9 million in the second quarter of 2026 compared with $1.1 million in the second quarter of 2025. The year-over-year increase was primarily driven by our Buy and Host one-stop solution, which continued to attract clients seeking asset ownership with simplified, hassle-free mining operations. Cost of Revenue Cost of revenue in the second quarter of 2026 was $43.7 million, a decrease of 57.4% from $102.5 million in the second quarter of 2025. The decrease was mainly attributable to a reduction in scale. Operating Expenses Sales and marketing expenses in the second quarter of 2026 were US$1.2 million, a significant increase from US$0.6 million in the same period of 2025. Sales and marketing expenses included share-based compensation expenses of US$0.9 million, compared to less than US$0.1 million during the same period last year. General and administrative expenses, and research and development expenses for the second quarter of 2026 were $2.2 million and $0.5 million, respectively. Excluding share-based compensation expenses of $0.2 million, these expenses were approximately in line with those in the same period of 2025. The Company recognized a $16.9 million fair value loss on digital assets and digital asset receivables or payables in the second quarter of 2026, reflecting downward pressure on Bitcoin prices during the period. By comparison, the Company recognized a $43.4 million fair value gain in the second quarter of 2025. Net (Loss)/Income Net loss in the second quarter of 2026 was $20.5 million, compared to the net income of $47.1 million in the same period of 2025. Adjusted EBITDA Adjusted EBITDA in the second quarter of 2026 was negative $18.4 million, compared to positive $60.7 million in the same period of 2025. Liquidity and Capital Resources As of June 30, 2026, the Company had cash and cash equivalents and digital assets of $119.5 million, compared to $177.1 million as of December 31, 2025. The decrease was primarily due to the decline in the fair value of Bitcoin held, the repayment of $10 million in Bitcoin-backed loans, and the prepayment made to secure hashrate procurement.
